lessons.title: Introduction to Version Control
lessons.description: Why Git and how it works

steps.content: Git is a distributed version control system. It tracks changes to files over time, allowing you to revert, compare, and collaborate. Every developer has a full copy of the repository (including history) on their machine. Changes are committed locally, then pushed to a remote (like GitHub).

Key concepts: repository (repo) = project folder with .git directory. commit = snapshot of changes with a message. branch = independent line of development. merge = combine branches. remote = server copy (GitHub, GitLab). HEAD = current commit pointer.

steps.question: What does 'distributed' mean in distributed version control?
options: Code is spread across multiple servers
Every developer has a full copy of the repository
steps.explanation: Distributed means each clone contains the full history. You can work offline, commit locally, and sync later. No single point of failure.

steps.question: A ______ is a snapshot of your changes with a descriptive message.
steps.explanation: A commit records changes to the repository. Each commit has a unique hash (SHA), author, timestamp, and message.

steps.question: Order these commands to initialize a Git repo and make first commit
steps.explanation: Initialize repo, stage all files, commit with message.

steps.question: Git tracks changes to individual files, not the entire project.
steps.explanation: Git tracks the entire project as a series of snapshots. Each commit represents the state of all tracked files at that point.

steps.question: What does HEAD refer to in Git?
options: The latest commit on the current branch
steps.explanation: HEAD is a pointer to the current commit (usually the tip of the current branch). Detached HEAD means pointing directly to a commit, not a branch.

steps.content: Git workflow: modify files -> git add (stage) -> git commit (save). Staging area (index) lets you choose which changes go into the next commit. git status shows working tree state. git diff shows unstaged changes. git diff --staged shows staged changes.

Viewing history: git log shows commit history. git log --oneline for compact view. git show <commit> shows details of a commit. git log -p shows patches. .gitignore lists files to ignore (build artifacts, secrets, dependencies).

steps.question: What does git add . do?
options: Stages all new and modified files
steps.explanation: git add stages changes for the next commit. The dot means all files in current directory and subdirectories. It doesn't commit.

steps.question: To see a compact one-line history, use git log --______.
steps.explanation: git log --oneline shows each commit on one line with abbreviated hash and message.

steps.question: Order to stage a specific file and commit with message
steps.explanation: Stage the specific file, then commit with a descriptive message.

steps.question: git diff shows changes that are already staged.
steps.explanation: git diff shows unstaged changes. git diff --staged (or --cached) shows staged changes.

steps.question: What should you add to .gitignore?
steps.explanation: Ignore build outputs (dist/, build/), dependencies (node_modules/, __pycache__/), secrets (.env), and IDE files (.vscode/). Never ignore source code.

steps.content: Branches let you develop features in isolation. git branch lists branches. git branch <name> creates branch. git checkout <name> or git switch <name> switches branches. git checkout -b <name> creates and switches. Main branch is typically 'main' or 'master'.

Merging combines branches. git merge <branch> merges into current branch. Fast-forward merge if no divergence. Merge commit if branches diverged. Conflicts occur when same lines changed differently - must resolve manually. git status shows conflicted files. Edit files, then git add, git commit.

steps.question: What command creates a new branch AND switches to it?
steps.explanation: git checkout -b <name> creates and switches in one command. git switch -c <name> does the same (newer command).

steps.question: When merging, if the same lines were changed in both branches, Git creates a ______.
steps.explanation: Git can't automatically merge when both branches modified the same lines. You must manually resolve by editing the file, then stage and commit.

steps.question: Order to merge a feature branch into main
steps.explanation: Switch to target branch (main), merge source branch (feature), push updated main.
hints: Be on the branch you're merging INTO

steps.question: A fast-forward merge creates a new merge commit.
steps.explanation: Fast-forward merge simply moves the branch pointer forward - no merge commit created. Only when branches diverged does a merge commit appear.

steps.question: After resolving a merge conflict, what commands complete the merge?
steps.explanation: Stage the resolved file(s) with git add, then git commit to complete the merge. Git will suggest a merge commit message.

steps.content: GitHub hosts Git repositories remotely. git remote -v lists remotes. git remote add origin <url> adds remote. git push -u origin main pushes and sets upstream. git pull fetches and merges. git fetch downloads without merging.

Pull Requests (PRs) are GitHub's code review workflow. Fork repo -> clone fork -> create branch -> push branch -> open PR from fork to upstream. Reviewers comment, suggest changes. CI runs tests. Merge when approved. Keep fork updated with upstream.

steps.question: What does git push -u origin main do?
options: Pushes main branch and sets upstream tracking
Creates a new branch called main
steps.explanation: -u (--set-upstream) links local main to origin/main. Future git push/pull work without arguments.

steps.question: The GitHub workflow for contributing to open source is called a ______ ______.
steps.explanation: Pull Request (PR) is a request to merge your branch into another repository. It enables code review and discussion before merging.

steps.question: Order to fork, clone, branch, and push for a PR
steps.explanation: Fork first, clone your fork, create feature branch, push to your fork, open PR to upstream.

steps.question: git pull is equivalent to git fetch followed by git merge.
steps.explanation: git pull = git fetch + git merge. It downloads changes and immediately tries to merge them. git fetch alone is safer for reviewing before merging.

steps.question: To update your fork with changes from the original (upstream) repo:
steps.explanation: Add upstream remote: git remote add upstream <original-url>. Then git fetch upstream && git merge upstream/main (or git pull upstream main).
